title: Diawa BG 2500 (classic)
text:
Diawa BG reel


There are lots of reviews on the Diawa BG. It’s a tried and true reel that is loved across the saltwater fishing community - particularly those looking for the most bang for their buck. Most reviews are for larger sizes, so I’m going to cover the inshore size - the 2500. I am sad to say I no longer own this reel - mine is now at the bottom of Mosquito Lagoon. This one hurt, as it was one of my favorite combos.
Let’s dive right into it. It’s an aluminum bodied reel with stainless steel bearings and a one piece handle with a paddle grip, which I prefer over other styles. It has a traditional bail wire, which I also prefer to Diawa’s air bail. It clocks in at 9.3oz - on the heavier side for a 2500, but still an acceptable weight for a do-it-all inshore reel in my opinion.
I bought this reel for the purpose of dock fishing and heavier inshore applications, however I ended up using it as my primary artificial bait setup due to issues with the Diawa Fuego I had originally bought for that purpose.
The BG has a lot going for it. It feels super solid when you hook into a fish. The carbon fiber drag works flawlessly. It’s surprisingly smooth for a heavy duty reel. I never had a single issue with this reel mechanically.
Initially I was skeptical about buying a saltwater reel without sealed bearings. Fishing from a kayak, you are bound to dunk your reels at some point when you’re leaning over the side to grab a fish. I’m happy to report I dunked this reel twice, and it never had any issues. I didn’t dissassemble, clean, and regrease it after it was underwater - I only sprayed it down with fresh water at the end of the trip. Which brings up my next point.
Diawa reels are not engineered to be servicable by the comsumer in my opinion. The BG has no fancy technologies like Diawa’s magseal, so it’s possible to do it, but they don’t make it easy. Parts are hard to impossible to find, so if that’s important to you it’s something to consider.
I did notice some arm fatigue after long days of casting artificials due to the weight. Not enough so that it would be a deciding factor when purchasing a reel for this purpose, but it is something to note. I’m also not a big fan of the bail action on the Diawa reels. When it clicks open, it doesn’t feel locked into place like a Penn or even a Shimano, but that’s a minor gripe. Those are really the only negatives I can think of for this reel. It’s a solid reel and there’s a reason its been in production for 10 years. The only reason I did not replace the one I lost with the exact same reel was for the sake of trying new things. I wanted to try a Shimano Spheros inshore.
In short, the BG 2500 is one of the best inshore reels I have owned and is at the top of my list of favorites. I will definitely be purchasing the new Diawa BG LT released this year to see if it lives up to the BG name. Tight lines!

title: Windy Weekend Conditions: October 31–November 1, 2026
text:
The forecast for Saturday, October 31, and Sunday, November 1, is calling for winds around 15 mph. I’ll be staying off the water this weekend.
In my experience, once the wind gets much above 10 mph, kayak fishing becomes more work than fun. It can be harder to control the kayak, stay on a spot, and make for an uncomfortable day of fishing.
If you decide to go, spot selection is critical. Look for a protected area with limited exposure to the wind rather than heading out onto open water. The wind is expected to come from the east, so I would be looking for an eastern shoreline here. One critical piece of planning is knowing your limitations - don’t get caught in a situation where you don’t have the strength or the ability to make it back. If you are just starting out, save your trips for days with lower wind speeds and work your way up to learn your comfort zone.

title: Real Florida Fishing
text:
About Real Florida Kayak Fishing
Welcome to Real Florida Kayak Fishing, a blog dedicated to sharing the experiences, lessons, and adventures that come with chasing fish from a kayak in the Sunshine State.
Whether you’re new to kayak fishing or a seasoned angler looking for fresh ideas, you’ll find practical information gathered from time spent on the water. This site covers fishing reports, kayak rigging and modifications, gear reviews, tackle recommendations, launch locations, and the countless lessons learned through trial and error.
The goal is simple: help fellow anglers spend less time figuring things out and more time catching fish. Every fishing trip teaches something new, and this blog is where those successes, mistakes, and discoveries are shared.
From inshore flats and backwater creeks to lakes and coastal waters, Real Florida Kayak Fishing is all about the pursuit of fish, the freedom and limitations of fishing from a kayak, and enjoying everything Florida has to offer.
Thanks for stopping by, and tight lines!

title: Penn Battle II 2500
text:
Penn Battle II reel


For my first review I am reviewing my oldest inshore reel - the Penn Battle II 2500. I purchased this reel in 2017 as a combo and considered it my first real inshore setup. My idea, at the time, was to get one solid reel with available replacement parts that would last forever.
Let me start by saying this reel has been fished harder than any other reel I own. It has been dropped in the sand regularly from bank fishing. It has been dunked no less than 5 times kayak fishing. It has been knocked around, sprayed with salt water, and everything you can think of that would be considered abuse for a fishing reel.
Let’s cover the good things first. The reel has served its purpose as a servicable workhorse. It is pretty much bullet proof. I have disassembled and regreased it 5-6 times over the years, mostly as a precautionary measure after trips when it was dunked. I replaced 1 bearing due to my inexperience servicing reels, when I tightened a nut down too much and crushed the bearing housing. Other than that, I haven’t had to purchase any replacement parts.
The drag on Penn reels is the best in the business. It feels smooth, sounds great, and adjustments are dialed in thanks to the wave spring construction. I have yet to replace the carbon fiber drag washers, which are readily available if you ever need to. I caught my biggest redfish with this reel: a 39 inch broad-shouldered monster with 10lb braid and a 20lb leader. The fight was at least 20 minutes with such light tackle, and it gave me 5 long, drag screaming runs. The drag never slipped and applied consistent pressure throughout the fight. Hundreds of fish have probably been caught on this reel, and the drag works good as new.
Next I’ll cover the bail action, which I also believe is the best out of the big 3 reel manufacturers. Flipping the bail open gives you a loud, positive click and feels like it is solidly in place - unlike the light mushy feeling of comparable Diawa reels. The wire is thick and durable, and it has never slammed shut on me during a cast, which cannot be said for other brands.
Now the bad.
Wind knots. This reel gets more wind knots than any reel I have owned. I’ve heard the argument that wind knots are never the reel and always a technique problem. Nonsense. I don’t get wind knots with any of my other reels at this frequency. It is a unquestionably a design issue. To mitigate this, you have to underspool the reel, which brings up my next negative:
Casting distance. This reel does not cast great. It’s not bad, but I get less casting distance than my other reels of the same size. This issue is compounded due to having to underspool it to prevent wind knots.
Weight. This reel is heavy compared to its competition at 10.3 ounces. It never really bothered me when it was my only inshore setup. But as I aquired more gear, I noticed it is my heaviest 2500. I fish 99% artificials, so I am casting all day. If you use a lot of live or cut bait, this is not an issue. Even on shorter trips with artificials, its not bad. But on a 6 hour day, it will wear you out.
So here’s where I sit with the Penn Battle II 2500 - if you are hard on your gear or want a reliable, servicable reel that will last you forever, especially if you use a lot of live or cut bait, this reel is for you.
If you are casting artificials all day on clear water flats where you need long, frequent casts, this will get the job done but may not be your best option.
One last thing I’d like to note, which I concluded from owning this reel, is the industries over-emphasis on needing higher end models if you are hard on your gear. They are constantly telling us if you dunk your gear you need IPX5 or IPX6 sealing, corrosion resistant coatings, etc. It’s not true. This reel isn’t IPX rated, and other than sealed bearings, doesn’t have any special sealing features, and it keeps on trucking.

title: Create a Digital Fishing Journal with Google Forms
text: Keeping track of your fishing trips can help you learn what works and improve your results. A digital fishing journal makes it easy to record catches, locations, weather conditions, and bait choices.

title: Create a Digital Fishing Journal with Google Forms
section: Why Use a Digital Fishing Journal?
text:
Why Use a Digital Fishing Journal?
Instead of keeping notes in a notebook, you can use Google Forms to record your fishing trips and Google Sheets to organize your data.
With this simple, free setup, you can:

Track fishing locations and dates.
Record fish species and catches.
Keep notes on bait, lures, and weather.
Review past trips and identify patterns.

title: Create a Digital Fishing Journal with Google Forms
text:
How to Get Started

1. Create a Google Form
Visit Google Forms and create a new form called “Fishing Journal.”
Add questions for the date, location, weather, bait used, fish caught, and any notes about your trip.


2. Connect Google Sheets
Open the Responses tab in your form and link it to a Google Sheet. Each form submission will be saved as a new row in your spreadsheet.


3. Record Your Fishing Trips
Open your form on your phone after each trip and enter your observations. Keep it simple so you can record information quickly and consistently.


4. Review Your Results
Over time, your spreadsheet will become a useful record of your fishing experiences. You can sort and filter your data to compare locations, baits, weather conditions, and catches.

title: Create a Digital Fishing Journal with Google Forms
text:
Start Tracking Your Fishing Adventures
A digital fishing journal doesn’t need to be complicated or expensive. Google Forms and Google Sheets provide an easy way to organize your fishing data and learn from past trips.
Start with a few basic questions and add more details as needed. The more consistently you record your trips, the more useful your fishing journal will become.
